title: Full jitter proved on the contract library's contracts alone, checked once and not again by the run
summary: The jitter of examples 147 and 148, proved with no contract of the agent's at all. The proof by the tool's own checker reaches the same three JDK calls it does not implement, and the tool's contract library closes each: its contracts for `Integer.numberOfLeadingZeros`, `new Random(long)` and `Random.nextInt(int)` were checked once, the first proved against the JDK's own bytecode and the other two tested on a real JVM, and the run applies them on the record of that check without checking them again. Under `--max-trust 0`, the policy CI uses, the proof may rest on no unchecked contract, and it rests on none.

change.description: Add `Jitter#fullJitterMillis`, full jitter for the retry filter: a wait drawn uniformly from zero up to the exponential backoff's ceiling, so that the clients one failure released together do not retry together. The ceiling is the base shifted left by the attempt, the shift stopped at the base's leading zeros less one (`Integer.numberOfLeadingZeros`) so that it never reaches the sign bit, then capped; the draw is `new Random(requestId * 31 + attempt).nextInt(ceiling)`, seeded so that a test or a replayed request log sees the same waits. The module's properties file gains the property that a wait is never negative and always below the cap, and that an invalid policy is refused with `IllegalArgumentException`. Four tests come with it, and pass.

risk: The wait is a shift, `baseMillis << shift`, which an `int` holds only while the base's highest one bit stays below the sign bit. Past it the ceiling wraps to a negative number or zero, `Math.min` keeps it since it is below the cap, and `nextInt` throws `IllegalArgumentException` on the retry path, which is the one path a retry filter must not fail on. The guard, the base's leading zeros less one, is easy to get one wrong. The tests try forty attempts of one policy, base 100; the property is about every base, cap and attempt, and a proof of it rests, for the three calls the checker does not implement, on what it is told of them.
explanation: The proof reaches `jdk-static-method:java.lang.Integer.numberOfLeadingZeros(I)I`, `jdk-constructor:java.util.Random.<init>(J)V` and `jdk-primitive-method:java.util.Random.nextInt(I)I`, each on JDK 25.0.4.1, and the example gives the tool no contracts file. Under `--gaps advised` a gap with no contract of the agent's takes the contract library's (`lib/models/contracts/`, built into the tool), which has one for each. Its record in `checked.json` says how each was checked, on which JDK and by which jvmcontract: the one for `numberOfLeadingZeros` proved against the bytecode of `java.lang.Integer`, whose class file still has the digest the proof recorded, and the two for `Random` tested on boundary and seeded random inputs. Each record holds (the same contract, the same JDK, the same class file), so the run applies the contracts with that evidence and runs neither a proof of them nor a JVM test. The checker then proves the property over every `int` base, cap and attempt and every `long` request id, as in example 148. The verdict reads `relying on 3 contracts for gaps of the tool's own checker, 1 proved, 2 tested`, and each contract's line ends `checked once, on JDK 25.0.4.1 by jvmcontract 0.1.0, and recorded in the contract library, not checked again by this run`. None is trusted, so `--max-trust 0` refuses none.
resolution: None needed. The verdict rests on the library's three contracts at the levels their records give, the same levels as the agent's contracts in example 148, without the agent writing them and without the run checking them.
notes: Example 148 is the same change with the agent's own contracts in `gaps.contracts`, which the run checks itself (a proof of one against the JDK's bytecode and a JVM test of all three, about 0.2 s). Here the example has no `approach.contracts`: the contracts are the library's, which an agent (the session that made the example, Claude Opus 5.5) wrote for step 3d of `llm-dlc/loops/sound-verdicts.md` from the JDK's documentation, and `jvmcontract gap-contracts --dir lib/models/contracts --record` checked once and recorded. Checked inline when the example was written, on the patched module, with the library's own run: the whole proof took about 0.08 s, and its work directory has neither `contract-proofs` nor `contract-tests`.

A record holds only for the contract it was made of (a digest over the gap and the contract's keys), the JDK it was checked on, and for a proof the class file in the JDK image. After a JDK upgrade none holds, and each run checks the library's contracts itself, with a `note:` saying why, until the library is recorded on the new JDK; the id names the JDK the contract was written for, and a contract written for another JDK is checked under the new one's id.

With `--no-contract-library` the run stops before solving with the three gaps and a template, as advised does with no contracts (step 3a). With a contracts file of the agent's, the agent's contract for a gap comes first, even when it is refused: in example 147 the agent's `nextInt` contract the JVM refutes goes back to the agent, and the library's is not applied in its place.

`approach.maxTrust` 0 passes `--max-trust 0`. A contract the JVM cannot test (one with a parameter of an object type, say) is trusted, and under that policy it would be refused, its gap going back to the agent before anything is solved. The library keeps only contracts that are proved or tested.

references.title: Brooker, Exponential Backoff And Jitter (AWS Architecture Blog, 2015): full jitter, a wait uniform in [0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt))
java.util.Random.nextInt(int) (Java SE 25): throws IllegalArgumentException if the bound is not positive
